Hook: On the twenty-sixth of April 1956 a converted wartime tanker, the Ideal X, left Port Newark for Houston. On its deck were fifty-eight truck trailers, lifted aboard by crane, with the goods still inside. Its owner, Malcom McLean, ran a trucking company. Loading a ship by hand, sack by sack and crate by crate, cost by his reckoning about five dollars and eighty-three cents a ton. Loading his boxes cost under sixteen cents. Today most manufactured goods that cross an ocean travel in such boxes, and trade has grown into something the theories of the last part could not explain.

Here is the result in 2019: the forty largest trade flows among twenty large economies, each line as thick as the trade along it. Two things stand out. The biggest flows run between neighbours: the largest of all is between Mexico and the United States, about 594 billion dollars a year. And the rich economies trade enormous amounts with each other, Germany with France, Japan with America, often in the same kinds of goods. Neither fits the theories of Part thirty-five, which predict trade between countries that differ. In all, the world traded about 18 trillion dollars of goods that year.

This part's question: why is most trade between similar countries, and what did a generation of imports from China do? Why do similar countries trade similar goods? Why does trade fall so fast with distance, and stop at borders? Why do so few firms export, and what happens to the rest? And what did the surge of imports from China do to the American towns that made the same things?
Economics, Built. Part thirty-six: scale, firms and gravity.

Here is the plan. Trade in cars for cars, and the theory of variety and scale that explains it. A game of guessing trade flows, and the most successful equation in economics, gravity. Firms: why exporters are rare, and what trade does to the rest, with two models that put firms and countries together. One formula for the gains from trade, and a counterfactual computed on real trade data. And the evidence: the China shock, the tariffs of 2018 and 2025, value chains, and three dials.
Intra: Part thirty-five ended on a fact that its theories could not explain. Measure how much of a country's trade in a category runs both ways: the Grubel-Lloyd index, one when exports equal imports and zero when trade runs one way. Here it is for America's trade in capital goods, cars and consumer goods since 1967. In 1967, two years after the Auto Pact with Canada, America's trade in cars and parts scored 0.93: it shipped cars north and bought cars back. In 2025 America exported 713 billion dollars of capital goods and imported 1133 billion. Herbert Grubel and Peter Lloyd showed in 1975 that much of rich countries' trade is like this, and that it is not an artefact of lumping different goods together. Neither Ricardo nor Heckscher and Ohlin predicts it: a country should not export and import the same thing.
Krugman: In 1979 a young Paul Krugman offered a third reason to trade, which needs no difference between countries at all. People like variety: not just more cars, but different cars. But each variety has a fixed cost of design and tooling, so it pays to make each in one place, by one firm. A market of 1000 workers on the Island can support only 250 varieties. Put two such islands together and buyers in both choose among 500. With an elasticity of substitution of 4, that raises real wages by 26 percent, though every firm sells the same amount at the same markup as before. Each country exports some varieties and imports others of the same good: cars for cars.

Add shipping costs and something else appears. If firms located in proportion to demand, the line would be the dashed diagonal. In fact the larger market gets more than its share of the industry, because firms that must pick one place to produce pick the one where most of their buyers are. With fifty-five percent of demand, the Island has 59 percent of the firms. So the larger country ends up exporting the good it most wants. Krugman called it the home-market effect: here demand creates comparative advantage, rather than the other way round.
PlayIt: Chapter three. Play it: guess the trade.

Your turn. In 2019, to which of these three countries did Spain sell the most goods? Portugal, its small neighbour, with a GDP of a quarter of a trillion dollars; Japan, twenty times as large and ten thousand kilometres away; or Brazil, nearly eight times as large, Portuguese-speaking and Latin American. Pause, and choose.

The answer is A, by far. Spain sold Portugal 26 billion dollars of goods, Japan 3.2 billion and Brazil 3.0 billion. A country one twentieth the size of Japan, but next door, buys eight times as much. The white bars are what one equation predicts from nothing but the two countries' sizes, the distance between them, whether they share a border and whether they share a language. It gets all three close. Trade is proportional to the product of the sizes, and falls with distance. That is gravity.
Gravity: In 1962 the Dutch economist Jan Tinbergen noticed that trade between two countries behaves like Newton's gravity: it grows with their sizes and falls with the distance between them. Here are Germany's exports in 2019 to each of its partners, divided by the partner's GDP, against distance, both on log scales. The cloud falls along a line with a slope of -1.09: twice as far, roughly half the trade, even though shipping a container twice as far does not cost twice as much. Every country's exports look like this. Gravity is the most reliable regularity in empirical economics.

Estimated on all 28,107 pairs of countries, the equation fits remarkably. By least squares on the logarithms, trade rises almost one for one with the importer's GDP, falls with distance with an elasticity of -1.18, and a shared border, a common language, a colonial past and a trade agreement each multiply it by about two or three. João Santos Silva and Silvana Tenreyro showed in 2006 that logarithms bias these estimates when errors vary with size, and proposed estimating the equation in levels by Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood, with a fixed effect for each exporter and importer. Then distance's elasticity is -0.71, and the other effects shrink. The method is now the standard.

Gravity also measures borders. In 1995 John McCallum used data on trade between Canadian provinces and found that, in 1988, provinces traded about twenty-two times more with each other than with American states of the same size and distance, across one of the world's most open borders. James Anderson and Eric van Wincoop showed in 2003 that part of the puzzle was a mistake: what matters is the cost of trading with a partner relative to all the others, which they called multilateral resistance, and for a small country like Canada that changes the answer a great deal. But the border effect that remains is still large. Borders matter for reasons tariffs do not capture: currencies, rules, networks, trust.
Firms: Until the 1990s, trade theory talked about countries and industries. Then Andrew Bernard and Bradford Jensen opened the American census of manufacturing plants. Exporters were rare: 10.4 percent of plants in 1976, 14.6 percent in 1987. But they were large, making over half of all shipments. And they were better: more productive, more capital-intensive, paying higher wages, and they were so before they started to export. Good firms export; exporting is not what made them good.

The Island's firms look the same, by construction of the model in the next chapter. Of four thousand would-be firms, 260 survive, lined up here from least to most productive. Only the most productive 18 percent export, the gold bars, yet they sell 67 percent of all output. On average they are 9 times as large as the firms that sell only at home.
Melitz: In 2003 Marc Melitz built the model. Firms are born with a random productivity, drawn here from a Pareto distribution: the curve is the share of would-be firms above each level. Producing has a fixed cost, so only firms above a cutoff survive. Exporting has a further fixed cost and shipping costs, so only the best of those export. Now open the economy. Exporters expand and bid up wages, and the bar for survival rises: 22 percent of the firms that survived alone now exit. The best 18 percent export and grow. No firm has improved, yet output has moved from the weakest firms to the strongest, and average productivity, and with it real wages, rise by 5.9 percent. Trade raises productivity by killing firms.

Lower the cost of shipping and both rise. The gain from opening grows as more firms find it worth exporting and the selection becomes sharper. The evidence agrees: after Chile's liberalization, Nina Pavcnik found productivity rose in its import-competing plants, much of it by reallocation; after the Canada-US Free Trade Agreement, Daniel Trefler found large productivity gains in the Canadian industries that lost protection, alongside real job losses in them.
Formula: Chapter eight. One formula, and a counterfactual.

Part thirty-five's formula for the gains from trade has a remarkable property. Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare showed that Krugman's model, Melitz's and Eaton and Kortum's all give the same answer from the same two numbers: the share of spending on home goods, and the trade elasticity. Here it is computed from 2019 trade data with an elasticity of four, for eight economies, counting domestic spending as GDP less goods exports. Large economies that trade little relative to their size, like America and China, would lose under three percent in autarky; open ones like Germany, Korea and Mexico around nine or ten. The models differ in how trade works, but not, at this level, in how much it is worth.

The same models answer what-if questions. Robert Dekle, Jonathan Eaton and Samuel Kortum showed in 2008 that a counterfactual needs only today's trade shares and the elasticity, solved in proportional changes: exact hat algebra. Suppose trade costs between America and China rose by 25 percent, about the size of a broad tariff. Solving for the new wages and prices in all sixteen regions of the 2019 data: America's spending on Chinese goods falls from 1.9 percent to 0.9. America loses 0.22 percent of real income and China 0.34; Mexico and Canada gain, as trade diverts to them. The numbers are small because the model is static and has no inputs crossing borders; Part sixty-six returns with richer versions.
China: Now the evidence that changed the profession's mind. China joined the World Trade Organization in December 2001. America's imports from China rose from 19 billion dollars in 1991 to 321 billion in 2007. Over the same years American manufacturing employment fell, from 17.3 million in 2000 to 11.5 million in 2010. But many things hit manufacturing at once: automation, the recession of 2008, and trade. A national time series cannot separate them.

David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found a way to separate them. They studied seven hundred and twenty-two local labour markets, commuting zones. Each zone's exposure to China depended on what it happened to make in 1990: furniture towns, toy towns and textile towns were hit; others were not. To keep American demand shocks out of the measure, they built it again from China's exports to eight other rich countries, which reflect China's own rise. The result: a thousand dollars more of imports per worker over a decade cut a zone's manufacturing employment, as a share of its adults, by 0.60 percentage points, with unemployment, disability claims and lower wages following. Across the country, conservatively, about a quarter of the decline in manufacturing employment from 1990 to 2007.

Why the instrument? On the Island's four hundred zones, with an effect planted at -0.6, least squares finds -0.44: industries where Islanders' own demand rose import more and employ more, which hides part of the damage. Using exposure built from other countries' imports recovers -0.58. Recent work, by Borusyak, Hull and Jaravel and by Goldsmith-Pinkham, Sorkin and Swift, shows what such shift-share designs rest on: many industry shocks that are as good as random. The China shock's estimates have held up when re-examined this way.
Tariffs: Chapter ten. The tariffs of 2018 and 2025.

Here is America's average tariff since 1929: customs duties as a share of the goods it imported. After the Smoot-Hawley tariff of 1930 it peaked at 19 percent in 1933. From 1947, round after round of agreements brought it down, to 1.6 percent by 2017. In 2018 and 2019 America raised tariffs on washing machines, solar panels, steel, aluminium and, in several rounds, on most imports from China, and its partners retaliated. The average nearly doubled, to 3.1 percent. In 2025 it jumped to 8.0, the highest since 1946.

The tariffs of 2018 and 2019 covered more than three hundred billion dollars of imports. Who paid? Part thirty-five's large-country argument says foreign sellers should cut their prices and bear part of the tariff. They did not: Mary Amiti, Stephen Redding and David Weinstein, and Pablo Fajgelbaum and coauthors, found that the prices foreigners charged did not fall, so the tariff passed in full to American buyers. The buyers of imports lost about 51 billion dollars a year; after counting the tariff revenue and the gains to protected producers, the net loss was about 7.2 billion, 0.04 percent of GDP. In 2025, with the average tariff at 8.0 percent, America's imports from China fell from 440 billion dollars to 309 billion. Part sixty-six measures what followed.
Chains: Much of modern trade is not in finished goods but in tasks. The iPhone of 2009 was designed in California, built from parts made in Japan, Korea, Germany, Taiwan and America, and assembled in China, which added about six dollars and fifty cents to each phone. Yet every phone shipped from China counted as a Chinese export at its full factory cost, about 179 dollars: in gross terms, Yuqing Xing and Neal Detert calculated, the iPhone added 1.9 billion dollars to America's trade deficit with China that year. Counted by value added, China's share of each phone was its six dollars and fifty cents of assembly, and the same trade showed a small American surplus. Chains like this make countries more productive and more fragile: a factory closed by a flood or a pandemic stops production everywhere downstream, the subject of Parts sixty-three and sixty-six.
